chapter: New York years and Manhattan School
title: The art of doubling
summary: The challenge of switching among saxophone, flute, oboe and bassoon and how he practised an hour on each.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Now, uh...where are you instrumentally? You’ve got, you’ve added flute the previous decade...
Had you uh included the oboe and the bassoon at this point, or is that, was that still to come?
Well, I included the oboe during the ‘50s.
Uh I studied bassoon in the ‘60s.

What’s the challenge in uh...I know as I, as I, as I jokingly say as a “fallen” tenor player that, I mean, certainly the embouchure is different for each instrument, but uh...what’s, what’s the challenge in being a, a musician with these instruments at, at your beck and call? Is, is there a, I mean technically, certainly, but–

Well, it’s the art, it’s called the art of doubling. I had a...a student, his name was Brian McLaughlin, he got his doctorates from Columbia, he’s now an executive at um...BMI. Uh I found for myself that uh when I was with Cannonball, I had to, to practice like the saxophone maybe an hour, and then the flute an hour, and the oboe an hour and the bassoon an hour to learn how to make these transitions, ‘cause it’s really called the art of doubling.
Interesting. Yeah, that, it’s got to be a...it’s a challenge, absolutely.
It is, but it can be done.
